desc:
A grid of letters is given as an integer matrix board: 1 stands for a, 2 for b, and so on up to 26 for z.

Count how many times the lowercase string word can be read along a straight line of the grid. A reading is fixed by a start cell and one of the 8 directions (left, right, up, down and the four diagonals). The letters of the word must sit on consecutive cells in that direction, and the whole line must stay inside the grid. Two readings are different when their start cell or their direction differs, so a palindrome such as aba is counted once from each of its two ends.

For example, in the board [[1,2,1],[2,1,2],[1,2,1]] (rows aba, bab, aba) the word aba can be read 8 times: along the top row, the bottom row, the left column and the right column, each in both directions.
hints: Treat every cell as a possible start and every one of the 8 direction vectors (dr, dc) (all pairs from -1..1 except (0, 0)) as a possible direction.
For a fixed start and direction the last letter would sit at (r + dr * (L - 1), c + dc * (L - 1)). If that cell is outside the grid, skip this pair at once; otherwise compare the letters one by one.
Stop comparing at the first mismatch. Add one to the answer when all L letters match. The cost is at most m * n * 8 * L character comparisons, and no cell needs to be marked as used.
editorial: There is no choice to make once the start cell and the direction are fixed: the line of cells is determined, so a direct check is enough. Loop over all cells whose letter equals the first letter of the word, over the 8 directions, discard the pairs whose end cell leaves the grid, and verify the remaining letters one by one, stopping at the first mismatch.

This is the straight-line cousin of the word-path problems that need real backtracking (where the path may turn). Writing the direct check first makes the difference clear: here no cell is ever reused and nothing needs to be undone. The work is at most 8 * m * n * L comparisons, and the extra space is constant.
